title: The fifth
hookLine: in Shia law, a fifth of yearly surplus is also due, half for the Imam's share through scholars, half for needy descendants of the Prophet ﷺ

lines: WHAT CAME IN, MINUS WHAT IT COST.
cards: A family in a Shia home sits down on a set day of the year with a notebook. Not their zakat day; another one.
They add up what came in over the year and subtract what the year cost: rent, food, school, the car repair, the gifts for Eid. Whatever is left, the surplus the year didn't need, they divide by five.
One part of five is not theirs to keep. Some goes, through the office of a senior scholar they follow, to the work of religion. Some goes to needy families descended from the Prophet ﷺ.

teach.h: ONE VERSE: A FIFTH OF GAINS.
teach.b: First, the verse. Surah eight, verse forty-one, speaks of whatever you take as gains, and says a fifth of it belongs to Allah and the messenger, to the near kin, the orphans, the needy and the wayfarer.

Both communities read the same verse, but read one of its words differently. Second, the Sunni reading. Sunni scholars read the verse about the spoils taken in war, a fifth of which was set aside for these purposes.

They also apply it to buried treasure someone finds: a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari gives found treasure a fifth. Beyond those, Sunni law asks zakat, not khums, of ordinary savings. Third, the Shia reading.
Twelver Shia scholars read the verse's word for gains broadly, as any gain, relying on reports from the Imams of the Prophet's family that apply it to a person's yearly profit.

teach.h: SHIA: A FIFTH OF YEARLY SURPLUS.
teach.b: So in Twelver Shia law, a fifth of the year's surplus is due, after the year's real expenses, alongside zakat. Their jurists divide it in two.
Half is the share of the Imam, given today through a senior scholar, a marja', to support religious learning and the community.
Half is for needy descendants of the Prophet ﷺ, who in this teaching may not receive zakat from those outside the family.
Fourth: both readings start from the same verse, and both send the share to the near kin, the orphan, the needy and the traveler.
The difference is in a word and in the scholars each community follows, and each gives its reasons. A friend who pays khums is following their law, as a friend who doesn't is following theirs.

how: Twelver Shia Muslims set a yearly khums date, calculate a fifth of the surplus left after the year's expenses, and pay it through the office of the marja' they follow; Sunni Muslims apply a fifth to found treasure and pay zakat on their savings.

games.q: you've found buried treasure in a field. according to the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, what share is due on it?
o: a tenth, like a rain-fed harvest.
games.why: a fifth. on found treasure, Sunni and Shia law both apply a fifth.

practice: Think back over the last year: what did it actually cost to live it, and what came that you didn't need to spend?
Without calculating, let the two pictures sit side by side, what the year needed and what was extra, and notice how the second one looks.
